title: The heart and the vessels: two pumps, one loop
goal: Trace blood through the heart's four chambers and valves and through the pulmonary and systemic circuits, explain how the heart feeds itself, and tell arteries, capillaries and veins apart.

steps.title: Four chambers, two sides
steps.text:
The heart is two pumps side by side. Each side has two chambers [[c:heart-chambers]]:

- an [atrium](g:atrium) on top, which receives blood;
- a [ventricle](g:ventricle) below, which pumps it out.

The **right** side receives blood back from the body and pumps it to the lungs. The **left** side receives blood from the lungs and pumps it to the rest of the body.

So blood passes through the heart twice on every full lap: once through the right side, low in oxygen, and once through the left side, rich in oxygen.

claims.text: The heart has four chambers: an atrium and a ventricle on each side. The right side pumps to the lungs, the left side to the body.

evidence.quote: The human heart consists of four chambers: The left side and the right side each have one atrium and one ventricle.
Blood flows from the right atrium to the right ventricle, where it is pumped into the pulmonary circuit.

steps.title: Pulmonary and systemic circuits, in series
steps.text:
The two sides drive two circuits joined end to end [[c:two-circuits]]:

right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary trunk → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body → venae cavae → right atrium

The [pulmonary circulation](g:pulmonary-circulation) only has to reach the lungs next door. The [systemic circulation](g:systemic-circulation) reaches every tissue, against much more resistance. So both ventricles pump the **same volume**, but the left one must make a much higher pressure, and its wall is much thicker [[c:lv-thicker]].

Because the circuits are in series, whatever leaves the left ventricle in a minute must also pass through the lungs in that minute.

claims.text: The pulmonary and systemic circuits are linked in series: right heart → lungs → left heart → body → right heart.

evidence.quote: There are two distinct but linked circuits in the human circulation called the pulmonary and systemic circuits.

The pulmonary veins conduct blood into the left atrium, which pumps the blood into the left ventricle, which in turn pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta and on to the many branches of the systemic circuit.

claims.text: Both ventricles pump the same volume, but the left ventricle works against higher resistance, makes a much higher pressure and has a much thicker wall.

evidence.quote: Both ventricles pump the same amount of blood, but the left ventricle must generate a much greater pressure to overcome greater resistance in the systemic circuit.

Although the ventricles on the right and left sides pump the same amount of blood per contraction, the muscle of the left ventricle is much thicker and better developed than that of the right ventricle.

steps.title: Same blood, two pumps
steps.problem: At 150 beats·min⁻¹ a rider's left ventricle ejects 110 mL per beat. How much blood passes through her lungs each minute?
steps: Flow out of the left ventricle = volume per beat × beats per minute = 110 mL × 150 = 16,500 mL·min⁻¹ = 16.5 L·min⁻¹.
The circuits are in series: every millilitre that leaves the left ventricle comes back to the right side and is pumped through the lungs.
So the lungs also take 16.5 L·min⁻¹: not half of it (the flow isn't split between the circuits) and not double (it is the same blood counted twice).

steps.title: Four one-way valves
steps.text:
Four valves keep blood moving one way [[c:heart-valves]]:

| valve | between |
|---|---|
| tricuspid | right atrium → right ventricle |
| pulmonary (semilunar) | right ventricle → pulmonary trunk |
| mitral | left atrium → left ventricle |
| aortic (semilunar) | left ventricle → aorta |

The tricuspid and mitral are the atrioventricular valves. Their flaps are tied by cords (chordae tendineae) to papillary muscles in the ventricle wall, which stop the flaps being forced back into the atria when the ventricle contracts [[c:chordae]]. The semilunar valves stop blood flowing back from the arteries into the ventricles.

claims.text: Valves between atria and ventricles (tricuspid on the right, mitral on the left) and at the exits to the pulmonary trunk and aorta (semilunar valves) ensure one-way flow.

evidence.quote: Located in each of these openings between the atria and ventricles is a valve, a specialized structure that ensures one-way flow of blood.
The valves at the openings that lead to the pulmonary trunk and aorta are known generically as semilunar valves.
The opening between the left atrium and ventricle is guarded by the mitral valve.
The right ventricle receives blood from the right atrium through the tricuspid valve.

claims.text: Chordae tendineae and papillary muscles stop the atrioventricular valve flaps being forced into the atria during ventricular contraction; the semilunar valves prevent backflow from the arteries.

evidence.quote: This prevents the flaps of the valves from being forced into the atria and regurgitation of the blood back into the atria during ventricular contraction.
At the base of the pulmonary trunk is the pulmonary semilunar valve that prevents backflow from the pulmonary trunk.

steps.title: How the heart feeds itself
steps.text:
Heart muscle has its own supply: the [coronary arteries](g:coronary-arteries), which branch off the aorta just after it leaves the left ventricle. The left one feeds the left atrium, left ventricle and septum. Used blood drains through the coronary sinus into the right atrium [[c:coronary-supply]].

Two features matter in exercise:

- Flow to the left ventricle's muscle peaks while it relaxes ([diastole](g:diastole)) and nearly stops while it contracts. A faster heart rate spends a larger share of each beat contracting [[c:coronary-diastole]].
- At rest the left ventricle already extracts 70–80% of the oxygen from its blood. In heavy exercise its oxygen demand rises about sixfold, met mainly by about fivefold more coronary flow (figures mostly from animal studies) [[c:coronary-flow]].

claims.text: The coronary arteries arise from the first part of the aorta; the left coronary artery supplies the left atrium, left ventricle and septum; the coronary sinus drains into the right atrium.

evidence.quote: The first portion of the aorta after it arises from the left ventricle gives rise to the coronary arteries.
The left coronary artery distributes blood to the left side of the heart, the left atrium and ventricle, and the interventricular septum.
The two major systemic veins, the superior and inferior venae cavae, and the large coronary vein called the coronary sinus that drains the heart myocardium empty into the right atrium.

claims.text: Coronary flow peaks when the heart muscle relaxes and nearly stops while it contracts; a higher heart rate increases the share of time spent in systole.

evidence.quote: However, coronary circulation is not continuous; rather, it cycles, reaching a peak when the heart muscle is relaxed and nearly ceasing while it is contracting.

The increase in heart rate also increases the relative time spent in systole, thereby increasing the net extravascular compressive forces acting on the microvasculature within the wall of the left ventricle, in particular in its subendocardial layers.

claims.text: The left ventricle extracts 70–80% of coronary oxygen at rest; the about sixfold rise in its oxygen demand in heavy exercise is met mainly by about fivefold higher coronary flow. The figures come mostly from animal studies; the right ventricle extracts less at rest.

evidence.quote: In contrast, in the right ventricle, oxygen extraction is lower at rest and increases substantially during exercise, similar to skeletal muscle, suggesting fundamental differences in blood flow regulation between these two cardiac chambers.

The approximately sixfold increase in oxygen demands of the left ventricle during heavy exercise is met principally by augmenting coronary blood flow (~5-fold), as hemoglobin concentration and oxygen extraction (which is already 70-80% at rest) increase only modestly in most species.

steps.title: Arteries, capillaries, veins

claims.text: Arteries carry blood away from the heart and branch into arterioles and capillaries, where exchange happens; venules and veins return blood to the heart. Pulmonary arteries carry blood low in oxygen.

evidence.quote: An artery is a blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart, where it branches into ever-smaller vessels.

Eventually, the smallest arteries, vessels called arterioles, further branch into tiny capillaries, where nutrients and wastes are exchanged, and then combine with other vessels that exit capillaries to form venules, small blood vessels that carry blood to a vein, a larger blood vessel that returns blood to the heart.
In contrast, in the pulmonary circuit, arteries carry blood low in oxygen exclusively to the lungs for gas exchange.

claims.text: Systemic veins hold about 64% of the blood volume at any one time.

evidence.quote: In addition to their primary function of returning blood to the heart, veins may be considered blood reservoirs, since systemic veins contain approximately 64 percent of the blood volume at any given time
Veins are more compliant than arteries and can expand to hold more blood.

claims.text: Contracting leg muscles squeeze nearby veins; their one-way valves let blood move only towards the heart (the skeletal muscle pump).

evidence.quote: As leg muscles contract, for example during walking or running, they exert pressure on nearby veins with their numerous one-way valves.
This increased pressure causes blood to flow upward, opening valves superior to the contracting muscles so blood flows through.

points: Four chambers: on each side an atrium receives and a ventricle pumps. Right side to the lungs, left side to the body.
The pulmonary and systemic circuits are in series: both ventricles pump the same volume each minute, but the left makes far more pressure and has the thicker wall.
Tricuspid and mitral valves sit between atria and ventricles, held by cords; pulmonary and aortic valves guard the exits.
The heart feeds itself through the coronary arteries, mostly during relaxation; with the left ventricle already extracting 70–80% at rest, more oxygen in exercise means more coronary flow.
Arteries go away from the heart, capillaries exchange, veins return and hold about 64% of the blood, helped by the muscle pump.

variants.stem: Which heart chamber receives the blood coming back from the body?

options.text: The right atrium
options.why: Right: blood from the body returns through the venae cavae into the right atrium.

options.text: The left atrium
options.why: The left atrium receives blood from the lungs, through the pulmonary veins.

options.text: The right ventricle
options.why: The right ventricle receives blood from the right atrium, not directly from the body.

options.text: The left ventricle
options.why: The left ventricle receives blood from the left atrium and pumps it to the body.

variants.stem: A red cell has just been pumped out of the right ventricle. Which heart chamber does it enter next?

options.text: The left atrium, after passing through the lungs
options.why: Right: right ventricle → pulmonary trunk → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium.

options.text: The right atrium, after passing through the body
options.why: The right ventricle pumps to the lungs, not the body; the body's blood comes back to the right atrium only after the left side has pumped it out.

options.text: The left ventricle, straight through the septum
options.why: In an adult heart no blood crosses the septum; the right and left sides are joined only through the lungs.

options.text: The aorta, after passing through the lungs
options.why: From the lungs blood first reaches the left atrium and left ventricle; and the aorta is a vessel, not a chamber.

variants.stem: Blood from a runner's legs returns through the inferior vena cava. Through which chambers, in order, does it pass before reaching the aorta?

options.text: Right atrium, right ventricle, (lungs), left atrium, left ventricle
options.why: Right: through the right side to the lungs, then the left side to the aorta.

options.text: Right atrium, left atrium, right ventricle, left ventricle
options.why: The atria don't pump into each other; each atrium empties into the ventricle on its own side.

options.text: Right ventricle, right atrium, left ventricle, left atrium
options.why: This puts the ventricles first; the atria receive the blood and pass it to the ventricles.

options.text: Left atrium, left ventricle, (lungs), right atrium, right ventricle
options.why: This swaps the sides: blood from the body enters the right side first.

variants.stem: Why is the left ventricle's wall much thicker than the right ventricle's?

options.text: It must make a much higher pressure to push blood round the body
options.why: Right: the systemic circuit has much more resistance than the short pulmonary circuit.

options.text: It pumps a much larger volume of blood with each beat
options.why: Both ventricles pump the same volume; the circuits are in series.

options.text: It pumps blood to the lungs, which resist flow the most
options.why: This swaps the sides: the right ventricle pumps to the lungs, the low-resistance circuit.

options.text: It feeds the heart muscle from the blood it holds
options.why: Heart muscle is fed by the coronary arteries, not by blood inside the chambers.

variants.stem: At 160 beats·min⁻¹ a cyclist's left ventricle ejects 120 mL per beat. How much blood passes through his lungs each minute?

options.text: 19.2 L·min⁻¹
options.why: Right: 120 mL × 160 = 19,200 mL·min⁻¹, and in series the lungs take the same flow.

options.text: 9.6 L·min⁻¹
options.why: This splits the flow between the two circuits. They are in series, so the lungs get all of it.

options.text: 38.4 L·min⁻¹
options.why: This adds the left and right sides; it is the same blood passing both pumps in turn.

options.text: 1.92 L·min⁻¹
options.why: Unit slip: 19,200 mL is 19.2 L (1 L = 1,000 mL).

variants.solution: Left ventricle output = 120 mL × 160 beats·min⁻¹ = 19,200 mL·min⁻¹ = 19.2 L·min⁻¹. The circuits are in series, so the same 19.2 L·min⁻¹ passes through the lungs.

variants.stem: During a 10 km race a runner's right ventricle pumps 100 mL per beat at 170 beats·min⁻¹. How much blood leaves her left ventricle into the aorta each minute?

options.text: 17 L·min⁻¹
options.why: Right: 100 mL × 170 = 17,000 mL·min⁻¹, and the left ventricle pumps the same as the right.

options.text: 8.5 L·min⁻¹
options.why: This splits the flow between the circuits. In series, both ventricles pump the full amount.

options.text: 34 L·min⁻¹
options.why: This adds both sides; it is the same blood pumped twice in one lap.

options.text: 1.7 L·min⁻¹
options.why: Unit slip: 17,000 mL is 17 L (1 L = 1,000 mL).

variants.solution: Right ventricle output = 100 mL × 170 beats·min⁻¹ = 17,000 mL·min⁻¹ = 17 L·min⁻¹. In series, the left ventricle pumps the same 17 L·min⁻¹ into the aorta.

variants.stem: At rest before a triathlon a triathlete's left ventricle ejects 80 mL per beat at 50 beats·min⁻¹. How much blood passes through his lungs each minute?

options.text: 4 L·min⁻¹
options.why: Right: 80 mL × 50 = 4,000 mL·min⁻¹, and the lungs take the same flow.

options.text: 2 L·min⁻¹
options.why: This splits the flow between the circuits. In series, the lungs get all of it.

options.text: 8 L·min⁻¹
options.why: This adds both sides; it is the same blood counted twice.

options.text: 40 L·min⁻¹
options.why: Unit slip: 4,000 mL is 4 L, not 40 L.

variants.solution: Left ventricle output = 80 mL × 50 beats·min⁻¹ = 4,000 mL·min⁻¹ = 4 L·min⁻¹. In series, the same 4 L·min⁻¹ passes through the lungs.

variants.stem: A scan shows blood leaking back from a cyclist's left ventricle into his left atrium each time the ventricle contracts. Which valve is not closing properly?

options.text: The mitral valve
options.why: Right: the mitral valve guards the opening between left atrium and left ventricle, so a leak there flows back into the atrium.

options.text: The tricuspid valve
options.why: The tricuspid is the matching valve on the right side, between right atrium and right ventricle.

options.text: The aortic valve
options.why: A leaky aortic valve lets blood fall back from the aorta into the ventricle as it relaxes, not into the atrium.

options.text: The pulmonary valve
options.why: The pulmonary valve sits at the exit of the right ventricle into the pulmonary trunk.

variants.stem: What do the chordae tendineae and papillary muscles do when the ventricles contract?

options.text: Stop the atrioventricular valve flaps being pushed back into the atria
options.why: Right: they hold the flaps so blood can't flow back into the atria during contraction.

options.text: Squeeze the ventricle walls to push the blood out
options.why: The ventricle wall itself does the pumping; the cords only anchor the valve flaps.

options.text: Pull the semilunar valves open at the exits
options.why: The cords attach to the atrioventricular valves, not to the pulmonary and aortic valves.

options.text: Carry the electrical signal from the atria to the ventricles
options.why: They are anchoring cords and small muscles, not the heart's conducting tissue.

variants.stem: At 190 beats·min⁻¹ in a sprint finish, why is blood flow to the left ventricle's own muscle harder to keep up?

options.text: More of each beat is spent contracting, when coronary flow nearly stops
options.why: Right: coronary flow peaks in relaxation; a higher heart rate raises the share of time spent in systole.

options.text: Coronary flow peaks during contraction, which gets shorter
options.why: This reverses the timing: flow peaks while the muscle relaxes and nearly stops while it contracts.

options.text: The coronary arteries come off the pulmonary trunk, low in oxygen
options.why: They come off the aorta, just after it leaves the left ventricle, so they get oxygen-rich blood.

options.text: The muscle feeds on chamber blood, which moves through too fast
options.why: Heart muscle is fed by its coronary arteries, not by blood passing through its chambers.

variants.stem: On a hard climb a rider's left ventricle needs about six times more oxygen than at rest. How is most of the extra oxygen supplied?

options.text: By much higher coronary blood flow
options.why: Right: coronary flow rises about fivefold, because extraction is already high at rest.

options.text: By taking a much bigger share of oxygen from each litre of blood
options.why: The left ventricle already extracts 70–80% at rest, so there is little room to extract more.

options.text: By taking oxygen from the blood inside the left ventricle
options.why: Heart muscle gets its oxygen through the coronary arteries, not from blood in its chambers.

options.text: By a large rise in haemoglobin concentration
options.why: Haemoglobin concentration rises only modestly in exercise; it can't cover a sixfold demand.

variants.stem: A runner's left ventricle extracts 70–80% of the oxygen in its coronary blood at rest. What does that imply for a 5 km race?

options.text: Extra oxygen must come mainly from more coronary flow
options.why: Right: with little spare extraction, flow has to rise, about fivefold in heavy exercise.

options.text: The heart can simply triple its extraction instead
options.why: Tripling 70–80% would exceed 100%: extraction can rise only a little.

options.text: Coronary flow can stay at its resting level
options.why: Oxygen demand rises about sixfold; at resting flow it couldn't be met.

options.text: The heart muscle gets its oxygen from lung blood directly
options.why: The heart is fed through its coronary arteries from the aorta, like other organs.

variants.stem: The pulmonary arteries carry blood low in oxygen. Why are they still called arteries?

options.text: Arteries are defined by carrying blood away from the heart
options.why: Right: vessels are named by direction of flow, not by how much oxygen they carry.

options.text: It's an old naming mistake; they are really veins
options.why: Veins carry blood towards the heart; these carry it away, so 'artery' is correct.

options.text: Their blood picks up oxygen before it leaves the heart
options.why: Blood loads oxygen only in the lung capillaries, after it has left the heart.

options.text: Arteries are the vessels with valves along their length
options.why: It is veins, especially in the legs, that have valves along their length.

variants.stem: In a cyclist's thigh, in which vessels does oxygen leave the blood for the muscle?

options.text: The capillaries
options.why: Right: capillaries are the exchange vessels between blood and tissue.

options.text: The arterioles
options.why: Arterioles control flow into the capillaries; the exchange itself happens in the capillaries.

options.text: The venules
options.why: Venules collect blood after it has passed the capillaries and given up oxygen.

options.text: The large arteries
options.why: Large arteries are thick-walled pipes that carry blood to the tissue, not exchange vessels.

variants.stem: At rest, where is most of the body's blood at any one moment?

options.text: In the systemic veins
options.why: Right: they hold about 64% of the blood; their stretchy walls make them a reservoir.

options.text: In the arteries
options.why: Arteries have thick, less stretchy walls and hold a much smaller share.

options.text: In the capillaries
options.why: Capillaries are many but tiny; they hold only a small share at any time.

options.text: In the heart's chambers
options.why: The chambers hold only a small share; most of the blood at any moment is in the veins.

variants.stem: Running uphill, how does blood in a triathlete's lower leg get back up to the heart against gravity?

options.text: Calf contractions squeeze the veins, and one-way valves let it move only upwards
options.why: Right: this is the skeletal muscle pump, which raises the pressure in leg veins.

options.text: The pressure from the heart alone pushes it all the way back
options.why: Pressure in the veins is low; the muscle pump helps them work against gravity.

options.text: The capillaries contract and pump it into the veins
options.why: Capillary walls are thin exchange surfaces with no muscle to pump.

options.text: The arteries' elastic walls pull it back towards the heart
options.why: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; returning blood travels in the veins.
